findings: v2 is a different paper from v1. v2 asks whether uncorrected batch effects harm federated learning, using federated k-means and federated random forest on four multi-center omics datasets, and finds that without batch-effect correction (BEC) federated k-means fails to recover the classes and leave-one-center-out random forest degrades, while within-client 70:30 splits stay near perfect. It also presents fedRBE, a federated version of limma removeBatchEffect that sends only aggregated intermediate matrices (secure multi-party computation, at least three clients per feature) to a coordinator and reproduces the pooled result to floating-point precision. The v1 abstract (title "fedRBE ...based on limma") described only the tool and claimed a maximum difference of 3.6E-13 from the centralized method; the batch-effect impact study is new in v2.
numbers: v2: max abs element-wise difference between fedRBE and pooled limma <=2.49e-13 on 4 real datasets; simulated (30 repeats x 3 imbalance scenarios) mean abs diff <=3e-15, max <=5e-13. Batch-specific variance 15-99% before BEC, about zero after. E. coli leave-one-center-out RF: median MCC 0 -> 1 with BEC. Federated k-means median ARI 0.7-1.0 after BEC. Quartet dataset: perfect MCC with or without BEC. Datasets: 118 E. coli samples/5 labs; ovarian microarray 6 studies (332 samples); ccRCC proteomics 3 labs (887 samples); Quartet 48 profiles as 3 clients. v1: max difference no greater than 3.6E-13.
locations: v2 abstract; Results sections "FedRBE yields the same results as centralized BEC" and "Federated BEC improves the outcomes of FL"; Table 1; Figures 2-4; Discussion. v1 abstract.
caveats: v2 cites ranges (ARI 0.7-1.0) in the text and gives per-dataset values only in Figure 4, which I did not read numerically. Exactness holds for removeBatchEffect only, not count-based RNA-seq. Per-round communication cost not quantified in the pages read; SMPC needs at least 3 clients. Supplementary tables S1-S4 not opened. Sample totals in numbers are my sums of Table 1 class counts (279+53; 457+430).

findings: ODAL is a one-shot surrogate-likelihood estimator for distributed logistic regression. The local site sends its local MLE to the others, each other site returns a gradient (ODAL1) or gradient plus Hessian (ODAL2), and the local site maximizes the surrogate likelihood. It is approximate, not exact, relative to pooled analysis, but close in simulation, and it needs one round of communication where the lossless iterative GLORE needs 5-9. The real-data test splits one hospital dataset into sites, so it ignores true between-site heterogeneity.
numbers: Per site to local site: ODAL1 p numbers, ODAL2 p*p+p numbers; GLORE p*p+p per iteration, 5-7 rounds in simulation, 6-9 (mean 6.7) on real data. Simulation, 500 replications: ODAL1 relative bias <0.5% (results text) and SE ratio 1.02-1.25; ODAL2 bias <0.1%, SE ratio <1.05; setting B bias <0.3% both. Real data (UPHS, 30,810 normal, 4,763 fetal loss, 13.43%), 100 medications: relative bias <10% for 85% (ODAL1) and 99% (ODAL2); example drug 72 OR pooled 0.93, local 2.82, ODAL1 0.49, ODAL2 1.02. K from 2 to 100 sites, local n=1000.
locations: Abstract; Methods (Algorithms 1-2, Eq 2-6, Figure 1); Simulation settings A and B (Figure 2); Results Figure 4, Figure 5, Table 1; Discussion and Limitations.
caveats: The abstract says ODAL1 bias <3% in simulation but the Results text says <0.5%; I report both and have not resolved it (Figure 4 not read numerically). Logistic regression only; low-dimensional p. Simulation sites differ only in sample size (r random), covariates are homogeneous. Supplement not opened.

findings: SCAFFOLD adds client and server control variates to FedAvg local steps to correct client drift under non-iid data. The paper proves FedAvg can be slower than SGD with heterogeneous clients, while SCAFFOLD converges for arbitrarily heterogeneous gradients and is robust to client sampling. This is an optimization method for iterative training, so it is approximate at any finite round and there is no pooled-estimate comparison. Each round each client sends both a model change and a control-variate change (Algorithm 1), roughly double the FedAvg payload.
numbers: Simulated quadratics (N=2): SCAFFOLD K=2 about 2x and K=10 about 5x faster than SGD, unaffected by gradient dissimilarity G in {1,10,100}. EMNIST logistic regression, N=100 clients, 20% sampled, rounds to 0.5 test accuracy at 0% similarity: SGD 317, SCAFFOLD 77/152/286/266 for 1/5/10/20 epochs, FedAvg 258/428/711/1k+. At 10% similarity SCAFFOLD 62/20/16/11. At 100% similarity SCAFFOLD 60/10/7/4. Client sampling at 0% similarity (0.45 acc): SCAFFOLD 143, 290, 790 rounds at 20%, 5%, 1% clients.
locations: Abstract; Section 4 and Algorithm 1; Theorems I and III with Table 2; Section 7 (Figure 3, Tables 3-5); Conclusion.
caveats: The doubled payload is my reading of Algorithm 1 line 13 (the paper does not state a factor in the text I searched). Evidence is on EMNIST and quadratic simulations, not omics; NN result flagged by the authors as preliminary. Table 5 not read numerically. Appendix proofs not checked.

findings: Studies federated linear prediction when centers record different feature subsets, assuming block-wise MCAR missingness and a shared (X,Y) distribution. A plug-in predictor built from component-wise aggregated second moments is consistent, needs one communication round (each center sends local sufficient statistics once) and generalizes zero-shot to an unseen center. An impute-then-ridge route gives finite-sample bounds, exact ridge in one round with O(d(d+1)) floats per center, or FedAvg-style iteration with O(d) per round that converges to that estimator as rounds grow.
numbers: Plug-in finite-sample excess risk of order sqrt(d^2/n) (Remark 2.5). Multi-shot imputation communication scales O(T d^2). Simulation: latent-factor model, p=3, Lambda=1, sigma=0.3, tau=0.5, K=50 centers with d=8 in Fig 1a, n=200 in 1b, d=100 and n=1000 in 1c; no numeric table of errors.
locations: Abstract; Section 2 (Assumption 1, Prop 2.1, Theorem 2.4, Remarks 2.5-2.6); Section 3 (exchangeable imputation, Theorem 3.2, federated ridge); Section 5 and Figure 1; Discussion.
caveats: Theory assumes homogeneity across centers (no covariate or concept shift); the authors say relaxing it is open. Results are read from Figure 1 qualitatively, no reported numeric accuracy. Only simulated data. Proofs in appendices not checked. Version read is v2 dated after v1; earlier version may differ.

findings: Linking attack that matches a gene expression profile to the genotype profile of the same person. The discriminative sequence model (DSM, a conditional random field built on the Li-Stephens HMM) predicts genotype sequences from expression using all GTEx eQTLs and beats two published Bayesian linkers (GNB, EBL). It was tested for same-cohort, cross-cohort, enlarged-candidate-pool, unknown-membership and reverse (genotype to expression) scenarios, on chromosomes 19-22 only.
numbers: GTEx train 450, test 138 muscle: DSM links 138/138 on 4 chromosomes, GNB 136, EBL 134. Cross-cohort train GTEx 588, test FUSION 292: all methods >99% on 4 chromosomes. Plus 292 GOT2D candidates: DSM 292/292. Plus 21,996 HRC candidates (22,288 total): DSM 273/292 (93.5%), EBL 267 (91.4%), GNB 260 (89.0%) on 4 chromosomes. Unknown membership (146 of 292 absent, 100 trials): AUROC DSM 0.887, EBL 0.809, GNB 0.799; FPR <1% at TPR 50%, 8% at TPR 80% (EBL 35%, GNB 34%). Reverse linking 4 chromosomes: DSM 291/292, MetaXcan Pearson 171, Spearman 97. Training cost 75 GB memory and about 6 h per window.
locations: Results subsections and Tables 1-3, Figures 2-5, Supplemental Table S1; Discussion (limitations).
caveats: The XML was parsed to text so the table cells of Tables 1-3 were not read directly; the numbers come from the Results prose. Attack uses genotype and bulk muscle expression, not spatial or histology data; reidentification relevance to predicted expression is not tested. Supplement not opened.
